content.content:
========= compute_features.training.ML 
Train machine learning or survival models with custom cross-validation

Description:

     This function trains several machine learning models using
     repeated k-fold cross-validation, with hyperparameter tuning, and
     supports both classification and survival tasks. It allows
     flexible cross-validation schemes, including:

        • Standard stratified k-fold cross-validation

        • Leave-One-Dataset-Out (LODO) stratified folds by cohort

        • User-defined custom fold construction via a
          ‘fold_construction_fun’

Usage:

     compute_features.training.ML(
       features_train,
       task_type = c("classification", "survival"),
       target_var = NULL,
       trait.positive = NULL,
       time_var = NULL,
       event_var = NULL,
       metric = NULL,
       k_folds = 10,
       n_rep = 5,
       LODO = FALSE,
       batch_var = NULL,
       file_name = NULL,
       ncores = NULL,
       return = FALSE,
       fold_construction_fun = NULL,
       fold_construction_args_fixed = NULL,
       fold_construction_args_tunable = NULL,
       seed = 123,
       preprocess = TRUE
     )
     
Arguments:

features_train: A data frame with samples in rows and features in
          columns.

task_type: Character. Prediction task type: ‘"classification"’ or
          ‘"survival"’.

target_var: Vector. Target variable for classification tasks: one value
          per sample, in the same order as the rows of
          ‘features_train’, without missing values.

trait.positive: Value in ‘target_var’ representing the positive class.
          All other values form the negative class.

time_var: Numeric vector. Survival/follow-up time of each sample, in
          the same order as the rows of ‘features_train’ (required for
          survival tasks).

event_var: Vector. Event indicator of each sample (1 = event occurred,
          0 = censored), in the same order as the rows of
          ‘features_train’ (required for survival tasks).

  metric: Character. Performance metric for model selection and tuning
          (classification):

            • ‘"AUROC"’ - area under the ROC curve (used when ‘NULL’)

            • ‘"AUPRC"’ - area under the precision-recall curve

          Survival models are always selected by the concordance index
          (C-index); ‘metric’ is ignored.

 k_folds: Integer. Number of folds for cross-validation. Default: 10.

   n_rep: Integer. Number of repetitions for repeated CV. Default: 5.

    LODO: Logical. If ‘TRUE’, the cross-validation folds are stratified
          by cohort and outcome, for Leave-One-Dataset-Out analyses
          (train on some cohorts, test on a left-out one). The cohort
          is not used as a predictor.

batch_var: Vector. Cohort/batch of each sample, in the same order as
          the rows of ‘features_train’. Required if ‘LODO = TRUE’. For
          classification, each cohort needs at least ‘k_folds’ samples.

file_name: Character. File name prefix used to save performance plots
          in ‘"Results/"’.

  ncores: Integer. Number of CPU cores for parallelization
          (cross-validation folds are processed in parallel). Default:
          ‘NULL’ (sequential). For classification with
          ‘fold_construction_fun’, the models are trained sequentially
          and ‘ncores’ is not used.

  return: Logical. Whether to save the cross-validation performance
          plots in ‘"Results/"’. Default: ‘FALSE’.

fold_construction_fun: Function. Optional user-defined function for
          fold construction. It is called with ‘data’ (the training
          features plus the outcome: a ‘target’ column coded
          ‘"no"’/‘"yes"’ for classification, ‘time’ and ‘event’ columns
          for survival), ‘folds’ and ‘bestune’. It must remove the
          outcome columns before building features. Must accept a
          ‘bestune’ argument:

            • ‘bestune = NULL’ - build the features of every fold (for
              every combination of the tunable arguments, if any) and
              save them. The function can run its own parallel workers
              for this.

            • ‘bestune provided’ - rebuild features on the full dataset
              using optimized parameters, and return a list with the
              features plus the outcome columns, any custom output, and
              ‘bestune’ (with tunable arguments: a data frame with the
              selected values of these arguments).

          The function should save each fold as ‘"Results/fold_<fold
          name>.rds"’, a list with:

            • ‘train_data’ - training features plus the outcome columns

            • ‘test_data’ - test features (plus ‘time’ and ‘event’ for
              survival)

            • ‘obs_test’ - observed outcomes of the test samples, in
              the order of the rows of ‘test_data’ (classification)

            • ‘rowIndex’ - row indices of the test samples in ‘data’

            • ‘fold_name’ - name of the fold

            • ‘params’ - data frame with the values of the tunable
              arguments used (only with tunable arguments)

          With tunable arguments, the file of a fold contains a list
          with one such element per combination.

fold_construction_args_fixed: List of arguments passed to
          ‘fold_construction_fun’ that remain fixed across CV and final
          training.

fold_construction_args_tunable: List of arguments passed to
          ‘fold_construction_fun’ for hyperparameter tuning.

    seed: Integer. Random seed for reproducible cross-validation: it
          fixes the fold assignment and the randomness in model fitting
          (e.g. random forest, bagging, boosting), including when
          running in parallel with ‘ncores’. Default: ‘123’. Use ‘NULL’
          to leave the random number generator untouched. Randomness
          inside a user-supplied ‘fold_construction_fun’ that runs its
          own parallel workers is not covered: seed those workers
          inside that function.

preprocess: Logical. If ‘TRUE’ (default), near-constant and highly
          correlated (|r| > 0.9) features are removed before training
          (see Details). The features must then be numeric. Use ‘FALSE’
          to train on the features as given.

Details:

     The function supports both classification and survival analysis
     pipelines via ‘task_type = "classification"’ or ‘task_type =
     "survival"’.

     Classification trains and tunes 11 algorithms with ‘caret’
     (‘treebag’, ‘rf’, ‘C5.0’, ‘glmnet’, lasso, ridge, ‘knn’, ‘rpart’,
     ‘svmRadial’, ‘svmLinear’, ‘xgbTree’). Survival trains and tunes 6
     models with ‘parsnip’ and ‘censored’ (Cox PH, elastic-net Cox,
     parametric AFT, conditional inference tree, bagged CART, oblique
     random survival forest). The best model is selected by the
     cross-validation ‘metric’ (classification) or C-index (survival),
     and trained on all training samples with its tuned
     hyperparameters.

     With ‘preprocess = TRUE’, near-constant features and, for each
     pair of features with an absolute correlation above 0.9, one of
     the two are removed. The outcome is not used. Without
     ‘fold_construction_fun’, this is done once on all training samples
     before the cross-validation, so the folds and the final model use
     the same features. The test samples are not involved:
     ‘compute_prediction()’ keeps the features of the final model.

     When ‘fold_construction_fun’ is provided, the features of each
     fold are built by that function, and the preprocessing is done
     inside each fold: on the features built on the training part,
     keeping the same features in the held-out part. The final model is
     trained on the features the function builds on all training
     samples, preprocessed in the same way. See
     ‘vignette("a5_custom_folds", package = "pipeML")’.

Value:

     A named list:

     Model The selected model, trained on all training samples.
          Classification: a caret ‘train’ object (tuned hyperparameters
          in ‘$bestTune’, performance per resample in ‘$resample’).
          Survival: a list with the fitted workflow (‘$Model_object’),
          the tuned hyperparameters (‘$bestTune’), the C-index per
          resample (‘$Resample_matrix’, with the name of the model in
          its column ‘model’) and the training data (‘$trainingData’).

     ML_Models All trained models. Classification: models that predict
          the same value for all training samples are excluded.

     AUROC_median, AUPRC_median Classification: median and MAD of the
          cross-validation AUROC and AUPRC of each model.

     C_index_median Survival: median cross-validation C-index of the
          selected model.

     Custom_output Only with ‘fold_construction_fun’: the custom output
          returned by that function on all training samples and, with
          tunable arguments, the selected feature parameters in
          ‘$Parameters’.

Examples:

     ## Not run:
     
     # --- Classification ---
     data(data_example_classification)
     X <- data_example_classification[, setdiff(colnames(data_example_classification), "target")]
     res <- compute_features.training.ML(features_train = X,
                                         target_var = data_example_classification$target,
                                         task_type = "classification",
                                         trait.positive = "1",
                                         metric = "AUROC",
                                         k_folds = 5,
                                         n_rep = 2,
                                         ncores = 2)
     res$Model
     res$AUROC_median
     
     # --- Survival ---
     data(data_example_survival)
     X <- data_example_survival[, setdiff(colnames(data_example_survival), c("time", "status"))]
     res_survival <- compute_features.training.ML(features_train = X,
                                                  task_type = "survival",
                                                  time_var = data_example_survival$time,
                                                  event_var = data_example_survival$status,
                                                  k_folds = 5,
                                                  n_rep = 2,
                                                  ncores = 2)
     unique(res_survival$Model$Resample_matrix$model) # selected model
     res_survival$C_index_median
     ## End(Not run)
     


========= compute_prediction 
Compute Prediction Metrics for a Trained Machine Learning Model

Description:

     Applies a trained model to a test set and evaluates it. For
     classification, it computes AUROC and AUPRC with bootstrap
     confidence intervals, and Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity,
     Precision, Recall, F1 score and MCC at each probability threshold.
     For survival, it predicts risk scores and computes the C-index.

Usage:

     compute_prediction(
       model,
       test_data,
       target_var = NULL,
       trait.positive = NULL,
       task_type = "classification",
       time_var = NULL,
       event_var = NULL,
       file.name = NULL,
       return = FALSE,
       n_groups = 2
     )
     
Arguments:

   model: The trained model returned as ‘$Model’ by
          ‘compute_features.training.ML()’ (e.g. ‘res$Model’).

test_data: A data frame of predictor variables for the test set (for
          classification, a matrix is also accepted). It must contain
          all the features of the model; other columns are ignored for
          classification.

target_var: Vector of true labels for the test set, in the order of the
          rows of ‘test_data’ (classification only).

trait.positive: Value in ‘target_var’ representing the positive class
          (classification only).

task_type: Character. Either ‘"classification"’ or ‘"survival"’.

time_var: Numeric vector of survival/follow-up times of the test
          samples, in the order of the rows of ‘test_data’ (required
          for survival tasks).

event_var: Numeric vector of event indicators of the test samples (1 =
          event, 0 = censored; required for survival tasks).

file.name: Character. File name prefix of the plots saved in
          ‘Results/’.

  return: Logical. Whether to save the plots in ‘Results/’ (ROC and
          precision-recall curves for classification, Kaplan-Meier
          curves by predicted risk group for survival). Default =
          FALSE.

========= compute_features.training.ML 
Train machine learning or survival models with custom cross-validation

Description:

     This function trains several machine learning models using
     repeated k-fold cross-validation, with hyperparameter tuning, and
     supports both classification and survival tasks. It allows
     flexible cross-validation schemes, including:

        • Standard stratified k-fold cross-validation

        • Leave-One-Dataset-Out (LODO) stratified folds by cohort

        • User-defined custom fold construction via a
          ‘fold_construction_fun’

Usage:

     compute_features.training.ML(
       features_train,
       task_type = c("classification", "survival"),
       target_var = NULL,
       trait.positive = NULL,
       time_var = NULL,
       event_var = NULL,
       metric = NULL,
       k_folds = 10,
       n_rep = 5,
       LODO = FALSE,
       batch_var = NULL,
       file_name = NULL,
       ncores = NULL,
       return = FALSE,
       fold_construction_fun = NULL,
       fold_construction_args_fixed = NULL,
       fold_construction_args_tunable = NULL,
       seed = 123,
       preprocess = TRUE
     )
     
Arguments:

features_train: A data frame with samples in rows and features in
          columns.

task_type: Character. Prediction task type: ‘"classification"’ or
          ‘"survival"’.

target_var: Vector. Target variable for classification tasks: one value
          per sample, in the same order as the rows of
          ‘features_train’, without missing values.

trait.positive: Value in ‘target_var’ representing the positive class.
          All other values form the negative class.

time_var: Numeric vector. Survival/follow-up time of each sample, in
          the same order as the rows of ‘features_train’ (required for
          survival tasks).

event_var: Vector. Event indicator of each sample (1 = event occurred,
          0 = censored), in the same order as the rows of
          ‘features_train’ (required for survival tasks).

  metric: Character. Performance metric for model selection and tuning
          (classification):

            • ‘"AUROC"’ - area under the ROC curve (used when ‘NULL’)

            • ‘"AUPRC"’ - area under the precision-recall curve

          Survival models are always selected by the concordance index
          (C-index); ‘metric’ is ignored.

 k_folds: Integer. Number of folds for cross-validation. Default: 10.

   n_rep: Integer. Number of repetitions for repeated CV. Default: 5.

    LODO: Logical. If ‘TRUE’, the cross-validation folds are stratified
          by cohort and outcome, for Leave-One-Dataset-Out analyses
          (train on some cohorts, test on a left-out one). The cohort
          is not used as a predictor.

batch_var: Vector. Cohort/batch of each sample, in the same order as
          the rows of ‘features_train’. Required if ‘LODO = TRUE’. For
          classification, each cohort needs at least ‘k_folds’ samples.

file_name: Character. File name prefix used to save performance plots
          in ‘"Results/"’.

  ncores: Integer. Number of CPU cores for parallelization
          (cross-validation folds are processed in parallel). Default:
          ‘NULL’ (sequential). For classification with
          ‘fold_construction_fun’, the models are trained sequentially
          and ‘ncores’ is not used.

  return: Logical. Whether to save the cross-validation performance
          plots in ‘"Results/"’. Default: ‘FALSE’.

fold_construction_fun: Function. Optional user-defined function for
          fold construction. It is called with ‘data’ (the training
          features plus the outcome: a ‘target’ column coded
          ‘"no"’/‘"yes"’ for classification, ‘time’ and ‘event’ columns
          for survival), ‘folds’ and ‘bestune’. It must remove the
          outcome columns before building features. Must accept a
          ‘bestune’ argument:

            • ‘bestune = NULL’ - build the features of every fold (for
              every combination of the tunable arguments, if any) and
              save them. The function can run its own parallel workers
              for this.

            • ‘bestune provided’ - rebuild features on the full dataset
              using optimized parameters, and return a list with the
              features plus the outcome columns, any custom output, and
              ‘bestune’ (with tunable arguments: a data frame with the
              selected values of these arguments).

          The function should save each fold as ‘"Results/fold_<fold
          name>.rds"’, a list with:

            • ‘train_data’ - training features plus the outcome columns

            • ‘test_data’ - test features (plus ‘time’ and ‘event’ for
              survival)

            • ‘obs_test’ - observed outcomes of the test samples, in
              the order of the rows of ‘test_data’ (classification)

            • ‘rowIndex’ - row indices of the test samples in ‘data’

            • ‘fold_name’ - name of the fold

            • ‘params’ - data frame with the values of the tunable
              arguments used (only with tunable arguments)

          With tunable arguments, the file of a fold contains a list
          with one such element per combination.

fold_construction_args_fixed: List of arguments passed to
          ‘fold_construction_fun’ that remain fixed across CV and final
          training.

fold_construction_args_tunable: List of arguments passed to
          ‘fold_construction_fun’ for hyperparameter tuning.

    seed: Integer. Random seed for reproducible cross-validation: it
          fixes the fold assignment and the randomness in model fitting
          (e.g. random forest, bagging, boosting), including when
          running in parallel with ‘ncores’. Default: ‘123’. Use ‘NULL’
          to leave the random number generator untouched. Randomness
          inside a user-supplied ‘fold_construction_fun’ that runs its
          own parallel workers is not covered: seed those workers
          inside that function.

preprocess: Logical. If ‘TRUE’ (default), near-constant and highly
          correlated (|r| > 0.9) features are removed before training
          (see Details). The features must then be numeric. Use ‘FALSE’
          to train on the features as given.

Details:

     The function supports both classification and survival analysis
     pipelines via ‘task_type = "classification"’ or ‘task_type =
     "survival"’.

     Classification trains and tunes 11 algorithms with ‘caret’
     (‘treebag’, ‘rf’, ‘C5.0’, ‘glmnet’, lasso, ridge, ‘knn’, ‘rpart’,
     ‘svmRadial’, ‘svmLinear’, ‘xgbTree’). Survival trains and tunes 6
     models with ‘parsnip’ and ‘censored’ (Cox PH, elastic-net Cox,
     parametric AFT, conditional inference tree, bagged CART, oblique
     random survival forest). The best model is selected by the
     cross-validation ‘metric’ (classification) or C-index (survival),
     and trained on all training samples with its tuned
     hyperparameters.

     With ‘preprocess = TRUE’, near-constant features and, for each
     pair of features with an absolute correlation above 0.9, one of
     the two are removed. The outcome is not used. Without
     ‘fold_construction_fun’, this is done once on all training samples
     before the cross-validation, so the folds and the final model use
     the same features. The test samples are not involved:
     ‘compute_prediction()’ keeps the features of the final model.

     When ‘fold_construction_fun’ is provided, the features of each
     fold are built by that function, and the preprocessing is done
     inside each fold: on the features built on the training part,
     keeping the same features in the held-out part. The final model is
     trained on the features the function builds on all training
     samples, preprocessed in the same way. See
     ‘vignette("a5_custom_folds", package = "pipeML")’.

Value:

     A named list:

     Model The selected model, trained on all training samples.
          Classification: a caret ‘train’ object (tuned hyperparameters
          in ‘$bestTune’, performance per resample in ‘$resample’).
          Survival: a list with the fitted workflow (‘$Model_object’),
          the tuned hyperparameters (‘$bestTune’), the C-index per
          resample (‘$Resample_matrix’, with the name of the model in
          its column ‘model’) and the training data (‘$trainingData’).

     ML_Models All trained models. Classification: models that predict
          the same value for all training samples are excluded.

     AUROC_median, AUPRC_median Classification: median and MAD of the
          cross-validation AUROC and AUPRC of each model.

     C_index_median Survival: median cross-validation C-index of the
          selected model.

     Custom_output Only with ‘fold_construction_fun’: the custom output
          returned by that function on all training samples and, with
          tunable arguments, the selected feature parameters in
          ‘$Parameters’.

Examples:

     ## Not run:
     
     # --- Classification ---
     data(data_example_classification)
     X <- data_example_classification[, setdiff(colnames(data_example_classification), "target")]
     res <- compute_features.training.ML(features_train = X,
                                         target_var = data_example_classification$target,
                                         task_type = "classification",
                                         trait.positive = "1",
                                         metric = "AUROC",
                                         k_folds = 5,
                                         n_rep = 2,
                                         ncores = 2)
     res$Model
     res$AUROC_median
     
     # --- Survival ---
     data(data_example_survival)
     X <- data_example_survival[, setdiff(colnames(data_example_survival), c("time", "status"))]
     res_survival <- compute_features.training.ML(features_train = X,
                                                  task_type = "survival",
                                                  time_var = data_example_survival$time,
                                                  event_var = data_example_survival$status,
                                                  k_folds = 5,
                                                  n_rep = 2,
                                                  ncores = 2)
     unique(res_survival$Model$Resample_matrix$model) # selected model
     res_survival$C_index_median
     ## End(Not run)

========= replicate_deconvolution_subgroups 
Replicate deconvolution subgroups in a new dataset

Description:

     Reconstructs and applies deconvolution subgroup signatures based
     on a previous decomposition.

Usage:

     replicate_deconvolution_subgroups(deconv_res, deconvolution_test)
     
Arguments:

deconv_res: A list containing results from the deconvolution process,
          including:

            • ‘Deconvolution subgroups composition’: the member
              features of each subgroup, per cell type

            • ‘Deconvolution matrix’: the original deconvolution result
              used to determine relevant features

deconvolution_test: A data.frame or matrix of deconvolution results
          (e.g., from another cohort). If cell groups were aggregated
          with ‘aggregate_cell_groups()’ before computing ‘deconv_res’,
          aggregate the same groups here first; otherwise their
          features are missing and are set to ‘NA’.

Value:

     A data.frame with the projected subgroup features proportions: the
     same features, in the same order, as the "Deconvolution matrix" of
     ‘deconv_res’. Each subgroup is the median of its member features.
     Subgroups with no member in ‘deconvolution_test’, and training
     features missing from it, are set to ‘NA’ with a warning; a
     warning also lists subgroups computed from only part of their
     members.



========= prepare_multideconv_folds 
Prepare folds for multideconv cross-validation with processed training
and test data

Description:

     This function processes a dataset for k-fold cross-validation
     using the multideconv framework. For each fold, it generates
     training and test datasets by computing deconvolution subgroups
     features from the deconvolution matrix. It also processes the
     entire dataset once to provide a final processed training set.

Usage:

     prepare_multideconv_folds(
       data,
       folds = NULL,
       bestune = NULL,
       ncores = NULL,
       cells_extra = NULL,
       corr = 0.7,
       corr_type = "spearman",
       zero_thr = 0.9,
       cv_thr = 0.1,
       batch = NULL
     )
     
Arguments:

    data: A data frame of deconvolution features (samples x features)
          plus the outcome, as given by pipeML: a ‘target’ column
          (classification) or ‘time’ and ‘event’ columns (survival).
          The outcome columns are not used to compute the subgroups;
          they are added back to the returned data.

   folds: A list of integer vectors indicating row indices for the
          training set in each fold. The test set is implicitly defined
          as the complement.

 bestune: Optional tuning object; when provided, folds are skipped and
          full-data processing is returned.

  ncores: Number of CPU cores for parallel fold processing.

cells_extra: Optional character vector of additional cell labels to
          include.

    corr: Minimum correlation threshold passed to
          ‘compute.deconvolution.analysis()’.

corr_type: Correlation type passed to
          ‘compute.deconvolution.analysis()’.

zero_thr: Maximum zero fraction passed to
          ‘compute.deconvolution.analysis()’.

  cv_thr: Minimum coefficient of variation passed to
          ‘compute.deconvolution.analysis()’.

   batch: Optional batch covariate passed to
          ‘compute.deconvolution.analysis()’.

Details:

     The function runs the ‘compute.deconvolution.analysis()’ function
     on each fold's training set and uses the trained projection to
     compute the test set representation. It also runs multideconv on
     the full dataset to return the complete processed training set.

Value:

        • When ‘bestune’ is ‘NULL’ (fold mode): invisibly, a named list
          of processed folds, each also saved to Results/fold_<fold
          name>.rds. Each fold contains:

            • ‘train_data’: Processed training data with cell group
              features and the outcome columns.

            • ‘test_data’: Test data projected into the learned cell
              group feature space (plus ‘time’ and ‘event’ for
              survival).

            • ‘obs_test’: True class labels (or survival time/event)
              for the test set.

            • ‘rowIndex’: Row indices corresponding to the test set.

            • ‘fold_name’: Fold name if provided in the ‘folds’ list.

        • When ‘bestune’ is provided: a list with the processed feature
          matrix for the full dataset (including the outcome columns),
          the full ‘compute.deconvolution.analysis()’ output, and
          ‘bestune’.

========= aggregate_cell_groups 
Aggregate cell types into groups

Description:

     Adds, for every method-signature combination, a new feature
     <method>_<signature>_<group> with the sum of the cell types of the
     group (e.g. Myeloid cells = macrophages + monocytes + dendritic
     cells). Cell types are only summed within the same
     method-signature combination, and the original features are kept.

Usage:

     aggregate_cell_groups(
       deconvolution,
       cell_groups,
       min_types = 2,
       verbose = TRUE
     )
     
Arguments:

deconvolution: Deconvolution output of compute.deconvolution() with
          features as columns and samples as rows

cell_groups: A named list: each name is a group and each element a
          character vector with the cell types to sum, written as in
          ‘get_cell_type_nomenclature()’ (e.g. ‘list(Myeloid.cells =
          c("Macrophages.M1", "Monocytes"))’). A group name can be a
          cell type of the nomenclature (e.g. ‘Myeloid.cells’):
          combinations that already estimate it are left as they are.
          Other group names must not contain _ nor the name of a cell
          type of the nomenclature. The cell types of a group should
          not overlap (do not list a cell type together with its own
          subtypes).

min_types: Minimum number of cell types of the group that a
          method-signature combination must have to be aggregated.
          Combinations with fewer are skipped (with 1, the group would
          be a copy of a single cell type).

 verbose: Boolean value to whether print the cell types summed in each
          method-signature combination and the reminder of how to use

## Step 1 - TME cell composition by multi-method deconvolution (multideconv)
## Run from the results/ directory: package side outputs are written to ./Results/

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(multideconv))

data_dir <- "../data"
out_dir <- "deconvolution"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

methods <- c("Quantiseq", "Epidish", "DeconRNASeq", "DWLS")

## Inputs are log2(TPM + 1) restricted to a shared gene set. Back-transform to TPM
## and rescale each sample to 1e6 over these genes so both cohorts are on the same scale.
load_tpm <- function(file) {
  x <- as.matrix(read.delim(file.path(data_dir, file), row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE))
  tpm <- 2^x - 1
  tpm[tpm < 0] <- 0
  sweep(tpm, 2, colSums(tpm), "/") * 1e6
}

for (cohort in c("Gide", "Riaz")) {
  tpm <- load_tpm(paste0(cohort, "_log2TPM.txt"))
  cat("\n#####", cohort, ":", nrow(tpm), "genes x", ncol(tpm), "samples\n")
  deconv <- compute.deconvolution(tpm, methods = methods, normalized = FALSE,
                                  doParallel = TRUE, workers = 8,
                                  return = FALSE, file_name = cohort)
  saveRDS(deconv, file.path(out_dir, paste0("deconvolution_", cohort, ".rds")))
  write.csv(deconv, file.path(out_dir, paste0("deconvolution_", cohort, ".csv")))
  cat(cohort, "deconvolution:", nrow(deconv), "samples x", ncol(deconv), "features\n")
}

## Step 2 - Train a response classifier on Gide TME features (pipeML), validate on Riaz,
## and explain it with SHAP values.
## Run from the results/ directory: package side outputs are written to ./Results/

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(pipeML)
  library(multideconv)
  library(ggplot2)
})

out_dir <- "model"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
set.seed(123)

## ---- Data -------------------------------------------------------------------
coldata <- read.table("../data/colData_all.txt", header = TRUE)
rownames(coldata) <- coldata$rna_id

deconv_gide <- readRDS("deconvolution/deconvolution_Gide.rds")
deconv_riaz <- readRDS("deconvolution/deconvolution_Riaz.rds")

clin_gide <- coldata[rownames(deconv_gide), ]
clin_riaz <- coldata[rownames(deconv_riaz), ]
stopifnot(!anyNA(clin_gide$Response), !anyNA(clin_riaz$Response))
cat("Gide:", nrow(deconv_gide), "samples |", paste(names(table(clin_gide$Response)), table(clin_gide$Response), collapse = " "), "\n")
cat("Riaz:", nrow(deconv_riaz), "samples |", paste(names(table(clin_riaz$Response)), table(clin_riaz$Response), collapse = " "), "\n")

## ---- Training on Gide -------------------------------------------------------
## Cell subgroups (correlated deconvolution features merged by multideconv) are
## learned inside each CV fold on the training part only, then projected onto the
## held-out part, so the CV estimate is not inflated by feature construction.
res <- compute_features.training.ML(
  features_train = deconv_gide,
  target_var = clin_gide$Response,
  task_type = "classification",
  trait.positive = "R",
  metric = "AUROC",
  k_folds = 5,
  n_rep = 10,
  fold_construction_fun = prepare_multideconv_folds,
  fold_construction_args_fixed = list(ncores = 3, corr = 0.7),
  file_name = "Gide",
  return = TRUE,
  seed = 123)
saveRDS(res, file.path(out_dir, "pipeML_training_Gide.rds"))

cv_perf <- data.frame(model = names(res$ML_Models), row.names = NULL)
cv_perf <- merge(cv_perf, data.frame(res$AUROC_median, check.names = FALSE), by.x = "model", by.y = 0, all = TRUE)
write.csv(res$AUROC_median, file.path(out_dir, "cv_AUROC_Gide.csv"))
write.csv(res$AUPRC_median, file.path(out_dir, "cv_AUPRC_Gide.csv"))
cat("\nSelected model:", res$Model$method, "\n")
print(res$Model$bestTune)
print(res$AUROC_median)

## Subgroup definitions learned on all Gide samples (used for the final model)
subgroups <- res$Custom_output
saveRDS(subgroups, file.path(out_dir, "deconvolution_subgroups_Gide.rds"))
comp <- subgroups[["Deconvolution subgroups composition"]]
comp_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(comp), function(cell) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(comp[[cell]]), function(sg)
    data.frame(cell_type = cell, subgroup = sg, members = paste(comp[[cell]][[sg]], collapse = "; "))))
}))
write.csv(comp_df, file.path(out_dir, "subgroup_composition_Gide.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

## ---- Testing on Riaz --------------------------------------------------------
features_riaz <- replicate_deconvolution_subgroups(subgroups, deconv_riaz)
model_features <- setdiff(colnames(res$Model$trainingData), ".outcome")
cat("\nModel features:", length(model_features), "| missing in Riaz:",
    sum(!model_features %in% colnames(features_riaz)), "| NA values in Riaz:",
    sum(is.na(features_riaz[, model_features])), "\n")
write.csv(features_riaz, file.path(out_dir, "features_Riaz.csv"))

pred <- compute_prediction(model = res$Model, test_data = features_riaz,
                           target_var = clin_riaz$Response, trait.positive = "R",
                           task_type = "classification", file.name = "Riaz", return = TRUE)
saveRDS(pred, file.path(out_dir, "prediction_Riaz.rds"))
get_curves(data = pred$Metrics, color = "model",
           auc_roc = pred$AUC$AUROC, auc_prc = pred$AUC$AUPRC,
           roc_band = pred$Curve_bands$ROC, prc_band = pred$Curve_bands$PRC,
           file.name = "Riaz_test")

auc_tab <- data.frame(metric = c("AUROC", "AUPRC"),
                      estimate = c(pred$AUC$AUROC$estimate, pred$AUC$AUPRC$estimate),
                      lower_95CI = c(pred$AUC$AUROC$lower, pred$AUC$AUPRC$lower),
                      upper_95CI = c(pred$AUC$AUROC$upper, pred$AUC$AUPRC$upper),
                      chance_level = c(0.5, mean(clin_riaz$Response == "R")))
write.csv(auc_tab, file.path(out_dir, "test_performance_Riaz.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(pred$Metrics, file.path(out_dir, "test_threshold_metrics_Riaz.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(sample = rownames(features_riaz), response = clin_riaz$Response,
                     prob_responder = pred$Predictions$yes),
          file.path(out_dir, "test_predictions_Riaz.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(auc_tab)

## Sensitivity analysis (NOT used for model selection): Riaz AUROC of every model
## trained by pipeML, to see how much the test result depends on the selected algorithm.
sens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(res$ML_Models), function(m) {
  p <- tryCatch(compute_prediction(res$ML_Models[[m]], features_riaz, clin_riaz$Response, "R"),
                error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(p)) return(NULL)
  data.frame(model = m, Riaz_AUROC = p$AUC$AUROC$estimate,
             lower = p$AUC$AUROC$lower, upper = p$AUC$AUROC$upper)
}))
write.csv(sens, file.path(out_dir, "sensitivity_all_models_Riaz_AUROC.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(sens)

## ---- Feature importance (SHAP on the final model) ----------------------------
shap <- compute_shap_values(res$Model, task_type = "classification", seed = 123)
saveRDS(shap, file.path(out_dir, "shap_values_Gide.rds"))
X_train <- res$Model$trainingData[, colnames(shap), drop = FALSE]

## Direction: Spearman correlation between a feature's value and its SHAP value
## (> 0: higher abundance pushes the prediction towards response).
## Univariate R vs NR Wilcoxon tests in each cohort check whether the effect replicates.
wilcox_dir <- function(x, y) {
  p <- suppressWarnings(stats::wilcox.test(x[y == "R"], x[y == "NR"])$p.value)
  c(diff = median(x[y == "R"], na.rm = TRUE) - median(x[y == "NR"], na.rm = TRUE), p = p)
}
importance <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(shap), function(f) {
  g <- wilcox_dir(X_train[[f]], clin_gide$Response)
  r <- wilcox_dir(features_riaz[[f]], clin_riaz$Response)
  data.frame(feature = f,
             mean_abs_shap = mean(abs(shap[[f]])),
             shap_direction_rho = suppressWarnings(cor(X_train[[f]], shap[[f]], method = "spearman")),
             Gide_median_diff_R_minus_NR = g[["diff"]], Gide_wilcox_p = g[["p"]],
             Riaz_median_diff_R_minus_NR = r[["diff"]], Riaz_wilcox_p = r[["p"]])
}))
importance <- importance[order(-importance$mean_abs_shap), ]
importance$direction <- ifelse(importance$shap_direction_rho > 0, "higher -> response", "higher -> non-response")
importance$same_sign_in_Riaz <- sign(importance$Gide_median_diff_R_minus_NR) == sign(importance$Riaz_median_diff_R_minus_NR)
write.csv(importance, file.path(out_dir, "feature_importance_SHAP.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(head(importance, 20))

## Plots: global importance bar plot and SHAP beeswarm of the top features
top <- head(importance, 20)
p_bar <- ggplot(top, aes(x = reorder(feature, mean_abs_shap), y = mean_abs_shap, fill = direction)) +
  geom_col() + coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("higher -> response" = "#1b7837", "higher -> non-response" = "#c51b7d")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "mean |SHAP| (probability of response)",
       title = paste0("Top TME features - ", res$Model$method, " trained on Gide")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10)
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "SHAP_importance_barplot.pdf"), p_bar, width = 9, height = 6)

long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(top$feature, function(f) {
  v <- X_train[[f]]
  data.frame(feature = f, shap = shap[[f]],
             scaled_value = (rank(v) - 1) / max(1, length(v) - 1))
}))
long$feature <- factor(long$feature, levels = rev(top$feature))
p_bee <- ggplot(long, aes(x = shap, y = feature, colour = scaled_value)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, size = 1.3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#2166ac", high = "#b2182b", name = "Feature value\n(rank)") +
  labs(x = "SHAP value (impact on probability of response)", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10)
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "SHAP_beeswarm.pdf"), p_bee, width = 9, height = 6)

writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), file.path(out_dir, "sessionInfo.txt"))

deconv_riaz <- readRDS("deconvolution/deconvolution_Riaz.rds")

cat("Gide:", nrow(deconv_gide), "samples |", paste(names(table(clin_gide$Response)), table(clin_gide$Response), collapse = " "), "\n")
cat("Riaz:", nrow(deconv_riaz), "samples |", paste(names(table(clin_riaz$Response)), table(clin_riaz$Response), collapse = " "), "\n")

## Cell subgroups (correlated deconvolution features merged by multideconv) are
## learned inside each CV fold on the training part only, then projected onto the
## held-out part, so the CV estimate is not inflated by feature construction.
res <- compute_features.training.ML(
  features_train = deconv_gide,
  target_var = clin_gide$Response,
  task_type = "classification",
  trait.positive = "R",
  metric = "AUROC",
  k_folds = 5,
  n_rep = 10,
  fold_construction_fun = prepare_multideconv_folds,
  fold_construction_args_fixed = list(ncores = 3, corr = 0.7),
  file_name = "Gide",
  return = TRUE,
  seed = 123)
saveRDS(res, file.path(out_dir, "pipeML_training_Gide.rds"))

write.csv(res$AUPRC_median, file.path(out_dir, "cv_AUPRC_Gide.csv"))
cat("\nSelected model:", res$Model$method, "\n")
print(res$Model$bestTune)
print(res$AUROC_median)

subgroups <- res$Custom_output
saveRDS(subgroups, file.path(out_dir, "deconvolution_subgroups_Gide.rds"))
comp <- subgroups[["Deconvolution subgroups composition"]]
comp_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(comp), function(cell) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(comp[[cell]]), function(sg)
    data.frame(cell_type = cell, subgroup = sg, members = paste(comp[[cell]][[sg]], collapse = "; "))))
}))
write.csv(comp_df, file.path(out_dir, "subgroup_composition_Gide.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

## ---- Testing on Riaz --------------------------------------------------------
features_riaz <- replicate_deconvolution_subgroups(subgroups, deconv_riaz)
model_features <- setdiff(colnames(res$Model$trainingData), ".outcome")

  library(pipeML)
  library(multideconv)
  library(ggplot2)
})

out_dir <- "model"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
set.seed(123)

## ---- Data -------------------------------------------------------------------
coldata <- read.table("../data/colData_all.txt", header = TRUE)
rownames(coldata) <- coldata$rna_id

deconv_gide <- readRDS("deconvolution/deconvolution_Gide.rds")
deconv_riaz <- readRDS("deconvolution/deconvolution_Riaz.rds")

## multideconv passes the data through data.frame(), which prefixes IDs starting
## with a digit with "X" (Gide): restore the original sample IDs
restore_ids <- function(deconv) {
  ids <- coldata$rna_id[match(rownames(deconv), make.names(coldata$rna_id))]
  stopifnot(!anyNA(ids))
  rownames(deconv) <- ids
  deconv
}
deconv_gide <- restore_ids(deconv_gide)
deconv_riaz <- restore_ids(deconv_riaz)

clin_gide <- coldata[rownames(deconv_gide), ]
clin_riaz <- coldata[rownames(deconv_riaz), ]
stopifnot(!anyNA(clin_gide$Response), !anyNA(clin_riaz$Response))
cat("Gide:", nrow(deconv_gide), "samples |", paste(names(table(clin_gide$Response)), table(clin_gide$Response), collapse = " "), "\n")
cat("Riaz:", nrow(deconv_riaz), "samples |", paste(names(table(clin_riaz$Response)), table(clin_riaz$Response), collapse = " "), "\n")

## ---- Training on Gide -------------------------------------------------------
## Cell subgroups (correlated deconvolution features merged by multideconv) are
## learned inside each CV fold on the training part only, then projected onto the
## held-out part, so the CV estimate is not inflated by feature construction.
res <- compute_features.training.ML(
  features_train = deconv_gide,
  target_var = clin_gide$Response,
  task_type = "classification",
  trait.positive = "R",
  metric = "AUROC",
  k_folds = 5,
  n_rep = 10,
  fold_construction_fun = prepare_multideconv_folds,
  fold_construction_args_fixed = list(ncores = 3, corr = 0.7),
  file_name = "Gide",
  return = TRUE,
  seed = 123)
saveRDS(res, file.path(out_dir, "pipeML_training_Gide.rds"))

write.csv(res$AUROC_median, file.path(out_dir, "cv_AUROC_Gide.csv"))
write.csv(res$AUPRC_median, file.path(out_dir, "cv_AUPRC_Gide.csv"))
cat("\nSelected model:", res$Model$method, "\n")
print(res$Model$bestTune)
print(res$AUROC_median)

## Subgroup definitions learned on all Gide samples (used for the final model)
subgroups <- res$Custom_output
saveRDS(subgroups, file.path(out_dir, "deconvolution_subgroups_Gide.rds"))
comp <- subgroups[["Deconvolution subgroups composition"]]
comp_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(comp), function(cell) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(comp[[cell]]), function(sg)
    data.frame(cell_type = cell, subgroup = sg, members = paste(comp[[cell]][[sg]], collapse = "; "))))
}))
write.csv(comp_df, file.path(out_dir, "subgroup_composition_Gide.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

## ---- Testing on Riaz --------------------------------------------------------
features_riaz <- replicate_deconvolution_subgroups(subgroups, deconv_riaz)
model_features <- setdiff(colnames(res$Model$trainingData), ".outcome")
cat("\nModel features:", length(model_features), "| missing in Riaz:",
    sum(!model_features %in% colnames(features_riaz)), "| NA values in Riaz:",
    sum(is.na(features_riaz[, model_features])), "\n")
write.csv(features_riaz, file.path(out_dir, "features_Riaz.csv"))

pred <- compute_prediction(model = res$Model, test_data = features_riaz,
                           target_var = clin_riaz$Response, trait.positive = "R",
                           task_type = "classification", file.name = "Riaz", return = TRUE)
saveRDS(pred, file.path(out_dir, "prediction_Riaz.rds"))
get_curves(data = pred$Metrics, color = "model",
           auc_roc = pred$AUC$AUROC, auc_prc = pred$AUC$AUPRC,
           roc_band = pred$Curve_bands$ROC, prc_band = pred$Curve_bands$PRC,
           file.name = "Riaz_test")

auc_tab <- data.frame(metric = c("AUROC", "AUPRC"),
                      estimate = c(pred$AUC$AUROC$estimate, pred$AUC$AUPRC$estimate),
                      lower_95CI = c(pred$AUC$AUROC$lower, pred$AUC$AUPRC$lower),
                      upper_95CI = c(pred$AUC$AUROC$upper, pred$AUC$AUPRC$upper),
                      chance_level = c(0.5, mean(clin_riaz$Response == "R")))
write.csv(auc_tab, file.path(out_dir, "test_performance_Riaz.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(pred$Metrics, file.path(out_dir, "test_threshold_metrics_Riaz.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(sample = rownames(features_riaz), response = clin_riaz$Response,
                     prob_responder = pred$Predictions$yes),
          file.path(out_dir, "test_predictions_Riaz.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(auc_tab)

## Sensitivity analysis (NOT used for model selection): Riaz AUROC of every model
## trained by pipeML, to see how much the test result depends on the selected algorithm.
sens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(res$ML_Models), function(m) {
  p <- tryCatch(compute_prediction(res$ML_Models[[m]], features_riaz, clin_riaz$Response, "R"),
                error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(p)) return(NULL)
  data.frame(model = m, Riaz_AUROC = p$AUC$AUROC$estimate,
             lower = p$AUC$AUROC$lower, upper = p$AUC$AUROC$upper)
}))
write.csv(sens, file.path(out_dir, "sensitivity_all_models_Riaz_AUROC.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(sens)

## ---- Feature importance (SHAP on the final model) ----------------------------
shap <- compute_shap_values(res$Model, task_type = "classification", seed = 123)
saveRDS(shap, file.path(out_dir, "shap_values_Gide.rds"))
X_train <- res$Model$trainingData[, colnames(shap), drop = FALSE]

## Direction: Spearman correlation between a feature's value and its SHAP value
## (> 0: higher abundance pushes the prediction towards response).
## Univariate R vs NR Wilcoxon tests in each cohort check whether the effect replicates.
wilcox_dir <- function(x, y) {
  p <- suppressWarnings(stats::wilcox.test(x[y == "R"], x[y == "NR"])$p.value)
  c(diff = median(x[y == "R"], na.rm = TRUE) - median(x[y == "NR"], na.rm = TRUE), p = p)
}
importance <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(shap), function(f) {
  g <- wilcox_dir(X_train[[f]], clin_gide$Response)
  r <- wilcox_dir(features_riaz[[f]], clin_riaz$Response)
  data.frame(feature = f,
             mean_abs_shap = mean(abs(shap[[f]])),
             shap_direction_rho = suppressWarnings(cor(X_train[[f]], shap[[f]], method = "spearman")),
             Gide_median_diff_R_minus_NR = g[["diff"]], Gide_wilcox_p = g[["p"]],
             Riaz_median_diff_R_minus_NR = r[["diff"]], Riaz_wilcox_p = r[["p"]])
}))
importance <- importance[order(-importance$mean_abs_shap), ]
importance$direction <- ifelse(importance$shap_direction_rho > 0, "higher -> response", "higher -> non-response")
importance$same_sign_in_Riaz <- sign(importance$Gide_median_diff_R_minus_NR) == sign(importance$Riaz_median_diff_R_minus_NR)
write.csv(importance, file.path(out_dir, "feature_importance_SHAP.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(head(importance, 20))

## Plots: global importance bar plot and SHAP beeswarm of the top features
top <- head(importance, 20)
p_bar <- ggplot(top, aes(x = reorder(feature, mean_abs_shap), y = mean_abs_shap, fill = direction)) +
  geom_col() + coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("higher -> response" = "#1b7837", "higher -> non-response" = "#c51b7d")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "mean |SHAP| (probability of response)",
       title = paste0("Top TME features - ", res$Model$method, " trained on Gide")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10)
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "SHAP_importance_barplot.pdf"), p_bar, width = 9, height = 6)

long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(top$feature, function(f) {
  v <- X_train[[f]]
  data.frame(feature = f, shap = shap[[f]],
             scaled_value = (rank(v) - 1) / max(1, length(v) - 1))
}))
long$feature <- factor(long$feature, levels = rev(top$feature))
p_bee <- ggplot(long, aes(x = shap, y = feature, colour = scaled_value)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, size = 1.3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#2166ac", high = "#b2182b", name = "Feature value\n(rank)") +
  labs(x = "SHAP value (impact on probability of response)", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10)
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "SHAP_beeswarm.pdf"), p_bee, width = 9, height = 6)

writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), file.path(out_dir, "sessionInfo.txt"))

# TME-based immunotherapy response prediction: train on Gide, test on Riaz

Scripts: `../scripts/01_deconvolution.R` and `../scripts/02_model.R`, both run from this directory.
Logs: `01_deconvolution.log` and `02_model.log`.

## Pipeline
1. **Deconvolution (multideconv 0.2.0)**: log2(TPM+1) was converted back to TPM and each sample rescaled
   to 1e6 over the 18,979 shared genes. Quantiseq, Epidish, DeconRNASeq and DWLS were run with the
   LM22, TIL10 and 5 CBSX scRNA-seq signatures. CIBERSORTx was not run because it needs credentials.
   This gives 284 features per sample. Each cohort was deconvolved separately.
2. **Training (pipeML 0.0.1)**: Gide, n=73 (46 R / 27 NR; PD1 and ipi+PD1). The positive class is R.
   5-fold × 10-repeat CV, tuned and selected by AUROC, across 11 algorithms.
   `prepare_multideconv_folds` rebuilds the multideconv cell subgroups (correlated method/signature
   estimates merged, Spearman r ≥ 0.7) on the training part of each fold only.
3. **Test**: The subgroups learned on all Gide samples were projected onto Riaz
   (`replicate_deconvolution_subgroups`), and the final model was applied to Riaz, n=51 (10 R / 41 NR, PD1).
   Riaz was not used for any training or model choice.
4. **Explanation**: SHAP values of the final model on the Gide training samples (`compute_shap_values`).

## Key results
| | AUROC | AUPRC |
|---|---|---|
| Gide CV (RF, median ± MAD) | 0.80 ± 0.10 | see `model/cv_AUPRC_Gide.csv` |
| **Riaz external test** | **0.59 (95% CI 0.40–0.78)** | **0.23 (0.16–0.45)**; chance = 0.20 |

On Riaz the model ranks responders a little above non-responders. The CI includes 0.5, so this is
**not significant evidence of transfer**. The other 10 algorithms give Riaz AUROCs of 0.33–0.65
(`model/sensitivity_all_models_Riaz_AUROC.csv`; this is a sensitivity check only, not used for selection).

## Files
- `deconvolution/`: raw deconvolution matrices per cohort.
- `model/pipeML_training_Gide.rds`: full pipeML output, including all models.
- `model/cv_AUROC_Gide.csv`, `model/cv_AUPRC_Gide.csv`: CV performance per algorithm.
- `model/subgroup_composition_Gide.csv`: which method/signature estimates make up each `*_Subgroup.N` feature.
- `model/features_Riaz.csv`: Riaz features in the Gide feature space.
- `model/test_performance_Riaz.csv`, `test_predictions_Riaz.csv`, `test_threshold_metrics_Riaz.csv`.

I built the model and ran it end to end: it predicts response well within Gide, but **that performance doesn't hold up on Riaz.**

## Results

| | AUROC | AUPRC |
|---|---|---|
| Gide, cross-validation (random forest, the model pipeML picked) | 0.80 ± 0.10 | – |
| **Riaz, external test** | **0.59 (95% CI 0.40–0.78)** | **0.23 (0.16–0.45)**; chance is 0.20 |

- **Riaz:** responders get slightly higher predicted probabilities than non-responders (median 0.54 vs 0.48). But the confidence interval includes 0.5, so this isn't evidence that the model works on a new cohort.
- **Choice of algorithm:** as a check only, I ran the other 10 trained algorithms on Riaz too. They score between 0.33 and 0.65, so no alternative clearly does better.
- **Likely reasons:**
  - Riaz has only 10 responders out of 51 patients.
  - Gide includes both anti-PD1 and ipilimumab + anti-PD1 patients; Riaz is anti-PD1 only.
  - Deconvolution estimates differ in scale between the two cohorts (e.g. Quantiseq M2 macrophages: 0.018 in Gide vs 0.057 in Riaz).

## Features driving the prediction
These rankings come from SHAP values on the final model. Features named `_Subgroup` are multideconv merges of estimates from several methods/signatures for the same cell type.

| Rank | Feature | Higher value predicts | Same direction in Riaz? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Monocytes (DeconRNASeq/TIL10) | non-response | yes |
| 2 | CD8 T cells (Quantiseq, DWLS, Epidish/TIL10 + NSCLC) | response | yes |
| 3–4 | M1 macrophages (LM22 and TIL10 subgroups) | response | partly (1 of 2) |
| 5 | CD8 T cells (LM22 subgroup) | response | yes |
| 6 | M2 macrophages (LM22 subgroup) | non-response | no |
| 7 | Cancer cells (Vanderbilt signature) | non-response | yes, significant in Riaz (p=0.04) |

The overall picture is consistent with known biology: CD8 T cells and M1 macrophages go with response, while monocytes, M2 macrophages and tumour cells go with resistance. Most top features differ strongly between responders and non-responders in Gide (p < 0.005). In Riaz, 7 of the top 10 and 16 of the top 20 point the same way, but only two reach significance there.

The SHAP values describe the model fitted on Gide, so treat the ranking as "what the model uses", not as confirmed biomarkers.

## 1. Input data transformation

- **What I did:** the files are log2(TPM+1). I converted them back with `2^x − 1`, set any negative values to 0, and rescaled each sample to sum to 1e6 over the 18,979 shared genes.
- **Where it applied:** only to the deconvolution inputs. I passed `normalized = FALSE` so multideconv would not re-normalize the data as if it were raw counts.
- **Why:** deconvolution methods expect linear-scale expression. The rescaling was needed because the per-sample sums were far from 1e6 and differed between cohorts:
  - Gide: about 41k to 730k
  - Riaz: about 830k to 1.27M
- **What I did not do:** I did not investigate why the sums differ. The rescaling was my own choice.
- **Downstream:** the ML features are the deconvolution outputs, with no further transformation. pipeML's default preprocessing (removing near-constant and highly correlated features) was applied.

## 2. Methods

**Run:**
- multideconv `compute.deconvolution` with Quantiseq, Epidish, DeconRNASeq and DWLS, across the 7 bundled `.txt` signatures:
  - LM22
  - TIL10
  - 5 CBSX scRNA-seq signatures
- pipeML `compute_features.training.ML`, using `prepare_multideconv_folds` to build features per fold. Internally this calls `compute.deconvolution.analysis` and `replicate_deconvolution_subgroups`.
- `replicate_deconvolution_subgroups` to project the Gide-learned subgroups onto Riaz.
- `compute_prediction`, `get_curves` and `compute_shap_values`.
- My own additions: Wilcoxon R-vs-NR tests in each cohort, and a Spearman correlation between each feature and its SHAP values to get a direction.

**Skipped:**
- CIBERSORTx: it needs credentials.
- Single-cell deconvolution and signature creation: no scRNA-seq data was provided.
- `compute.benchmark`: there is no ground truth.
- `aggregate_cell_groups`: it is optional.
- LODO cross-validation: there is only one training cohort.
- Survival modelling: there is no survival data.
- Cross-cohort batch correction, and the `batch` argument (for example, Gide therapy arm): not used.
- The files in the `signatures/MCPcounter/` subfolder: the package does not load them, because it only reads `.txt` files in the top-level folder.

## 3. Non-default parameters

**`compute.deconvolution`:**
- `methods` excluded CBSX, because there were no credentials.
- `normalized = FALSE`, because the input was already TPM.
- `doParallel = TRUE, workers = 3`: 3 workers for memory reasons, after 8 workers ran out of memory.
- `return = FALSE`: I saved the outputs to `results/deconvolution/` myself instead.

**`compute_features.training.ML`:**
- `k_folds = 5` instead of 10: with only 27 non-responders in Gide, 10 folds would leave about 2–3 per test fold.
- `n_rep = 10` instead of 5: for more stable CV estimates.
- `trait.positive = "R"`.
- `fold_construction_fun = prepare_multideconv_folds`: to avoid feature-construction leakage across folds.
- `fold_construction_args_fixed = list(ncores = 3, corr = 0.7)`: `corr` is the default value, and `ncores` was set for memory.
- `return = TRUE`, `file_name = "Gide"`: to save the plots.

**Other calls:** in `compute_prediction`, I set `return = TRUE` to save the plots.

**Not tuned:** the subgrouping thresholds (`corr`, `zero_thr`, `cv_thr`).

## 4. Problems

1. **Out-of-memory kill.** The first deconvolution run was killed during parallel DWLS with 8 workers; about 10 GB of RAM was already in use outside my job. I reduced to 3 workers and reran everything.
2. **Sample-ID mismatch.** The first modelling run failed because multideconv's `data.frame()` call had added an `X` prefix to Gide sample IDs. I mapped them back using `make.names()`; all 73 matched one-to-one.
3. **Garbled names in the per-algorithm check.** The printed row names came out as "2.5%", "2.5%1" and so on, because the AUC values were named vectors. The CSV was unaffected because it is written with `row.names = FALSE`. I added `unname()` to the script *after* the run, so the script on disk differs slightly from the version that produced the outputs.
4. **DeconRNASeq diagnostic.** It printed "number of cell types in the mixtures = 1". I noticed this and did not act on it.
5. **Riaz performance.** Riaz AUROC was 0.59, against 0.80 in CV. I reported this as is and did not tune anything in response. Linear SVM scored 0.33 on Riaz, below chance.
6. **Minor redundancies:**
   - ROC and PR curves were saved twice, as `*_Riaz` and `*_Riaz_test`.
   - The process looked like it was still running after it had finished; it then exited cleanly.

## 5. Checks

**Before deconvolution:**
- Both packages are installed, and I recorded their versions.
- All 73 Gide and 51 Riaz samples are in the clinical table, with no missing responses.
- Gene lists are identical between cohorts, with no NAs and no duplicates.
- The value range (0–14) is consistent with log2(TPM+1).
- I examined the low-library sample `8_PD1_PRE`: 4.6k genes above 1 TPM, and a Spearman correlation of 0.93 with the cohort mean.

**After deconvolution:**
- Both cohorts have identical feature columns and no NAs.
- I spot-checked Quantiseq values.

**Model and outputs:**
- All 151 model features are present in Riaz, with no NAs after projection.
- I inspected the subgroup composition of the top features.
- I looked at the SHAP bar plot.
- The logs contain no errors or warnings.

**Not checked:**
- I did not look at the beeswarm, CV or ROC PDFs.
- I did not compare training performance to CV performance, which the SHAP documentation recommends.
- I did not validate the deconvolution estimates against any reference.

## 6. Limits

**Riaz validation:**
- Riaz has only 10 responders, and the AUROC CI (0.40–0.78) includes chance.
- Prevalence differs a lot between cohorts (63% responders in Gide vs 20% in Riaz), so probability thresholds do not transfer.

**CV estimate:**
- The Gide CV AUROC of 0.80 is optimistic: it was used to select the best of 11 algorithms.

**SHAP interpretation:**
- SHAP describes how a random forest uses its own training data; it does not establish biomarkers.
- The correlated features split importance between them.
- The direction (Spearman between feature and SHAP) is a crude summary.

**Univariate tests:**
- The Wilcoxon p-values are not adjusted for multiple testing.
- "16/20 same direction" only counts signs, and many of the differences are tiny.
- Some top features are not significant even in Gide: NK resting p = 0.46, mast activated p = 0.90.

**Cohort differences:**
- Gide includes ipilimumab + anti-PD1 patients; Riaz is anti-PD1 only.
- Processing and scale differ between cohorts, and I did no harmonization.
- The subgroups were learned on Gide only.
- Response definitions were taken as given from the clinical table.

**Deconvolution:**
- Only 4 methods were used (no CIBERSORTx).
- The 1e6 rescaling over a filtered gene set affects methods that work on an absolute scale.
- The low Gide totals remain unexplained.

**Not checked:**
- I did not check whether any Gide patients appear in both treatment arms, which would leak information across CV folds.

  - Riaz: about 830k to 1.27M
- **What I did not do:** I did not investigate why the sums differ. The rescaling was my own choice.
- **Downstream:** the ML features are the deconvolution outputs, with no further transformation. pipeML's default preprocessing (removing near-constant and highly correlated features) was applied.

## 2. Methods

**Run:**
- multideconv `compute.deconvolution` with Quantiseq, Epidish, DeconRNASeq and DWLS, across the 7 bundled `.txt` signatures:
  - LM22
  - TIL10
  - 5 CBSX scRNA-seq signatures
- pipeML `compute_features.training.ML`, using `prepare_multideconv_folds` to build features per fold. Internally this calls `compute.deconvolution.analysis` and `replicate_deconvolution_subgroups`.
- `replicate_deconvolution_subgroups` to project the Gide-learned subgroups onto Riaz.
- `compute_prediction`, `get_curves` and `compute_shap_values`.
- My own additions: Wilcoxon R-vs-NR tests in each cohort, and a Spearman correlation between each feature and its SHAP values to get a direction.

**Skipped:**
- CIBERSORTx: it needs credentials.
- Single-cell deconvolution and signature creation: no scRNA-seq data was provided.
- `compute.benchmark`: there is no ground truth.
- `aggregate_cell_groups`: it is optional.
- LODO cross-validation: there is only one training cohort.
- Survival modelling: there is no survival data.
- Cross-cohort batch correction, and the `batch` argument (for example, Gide therapy arm): not used.
- The files in the `signatures/MCPcounter/` subfolder: the package does not load them, because it only reads `.txt` files in the top-level folder.

## 3. Non-default parameters

**`compute.deconvolution`:**
- `methods` excluded CBSX, because there were no credentials.
- `normalized = FALSE`, because the input was already TPM.
- `doParallel = TRUE, workers = 3`: 3 workers for memory reasons, after 8 workers ran out of memory.
- `return = FALSE`: I saved the outputs to `results/deconvolution/` myself instead.

**`compute_features.training.ML`:**
- `k_folds = 5` instead of 10: with only 27 non-responders in Gide, 10 folds would leave about 2–3 per test fold.
- `n_rep = 10` instead of 5: for more stable CV estimates.
- `trait.positive = "R"`.
- `fold_construction_fun = prepare_multideconv_folds`: to avoid feature-construction leakage across folds.
- `fold_construction_args_fixed = list(ncores = 3, corr = 0.7)`: `corr` is the default value, and `ncores` was set for memory.
- `return = TRUE`, `file_name = "Gide"`: to save the plots.

**Other calls:** in `compute_prediction`, I set `return = TRUE` to save the plots.

**Not tuned:** the subgrouping thresholds (`corr`, `zero_thr`, `cv_thr`).

## 4. Problems

1. **Out-of-memory kill.** The first deconvolution run was killed during parallel DWLS with 8 workers; about 10 GB of RAM was already in use outside my job. I reduced to 3 workers and reran everything.
2. **Sample-ID mismatch.** The first modelling run failed because multideconv's `data.frame()` call had added an `X` prefix to Gide sample IDs. I mapped them back using `make.names()`; all 73 matched one-to-one.
3. **Garbled names in the per-algorithm check.** The printed row names came out as "2.5%", "2.5%1" and so on, because the AUC values were named vectors. The CSV was unaffected because it is written with `row.names = FALSE`. I added `unname()` to the script *after* the run, so the script on disk differs slightly from the version that produced the outputs.
4. **DeconRNASeq diagnostic.** It printed "number of cell types in the mixtures = 1". I noticed this and did not act on it.
5. **Riaz performance.** Riaz AUROC was 0.59, against 0.80 in CV. I reported this as is and did not tune anything in response. Linear SVM scored 0.33 on Riaz, below chance.
6. **Minor redundancies:**
   - ROC and PR curves were saved twice, as `*_Riaz` and `*_Riaz_test`.
   - The process looked like it was still running after it had finished; it then exited cleanly.

## 5. Checks

**Before deconvolution:**
- Both packages are installed, and I recorded their versions.
- All 73 Gide and 51 Riaz samples are in the clinical table, with no missing responses.
- Gene lists are identical between cohorts, with no NAs and no duplicates.
- The value range (0–14) is consistent with log2(TPM+1).
- I examined the low-library sample `8_PD1_PRE`: 4.6k genes above 1 TPM, and a Spearman correlation of 0.93 with the cohort mean.

**After deconvolution:**
- Both cohorts have identical feature columns and no NAs.
- I spot-checked Quantiseq values.

**Model and outputs:**
- All 151 model features are present in Riaz, with no NAs after projection.
- I inspected the subgroup composition of the top features.
- I looked at the SHAP bar plot.
- The logs contain no errors or warnings.

**Not checked:**
- I did not look at the beeswarm, CV or ROC PDFs.
- I did not compare training performance to CV performance, which the SHAP documentation recommends.
- I did not validate the deconvolution estimates against any reference.

## 6. Limits

**Riaz validation:**
- Riaz has only 10 responders, and the AUROC CI (0.40–0.78) includes chance.
- Prevalence differs a lot between cohorts (63% responders in Gide vs 20% in Riaz), so probability thresholds do not transfer.

**CV estimate:**
- The Gide CV AUROC of 0.80 is optimistic: it was used to select the best of 11 algorithms.

**SHAP interpretation:**
- SHAP describes how a random forest uses its own training data; it does not establish biomarkers.
- The correlated features split importance between them.
- The direction (Spearman between feature and SHAP) is a crude summary.

**Univariate tests:**
- The Wilcoxon p-values are not adjusted for multiple testing.
- "16/20 same direction" only counts signs, and many of the differences are tiny.
- Some top features are not significant even in Gide: NK resting p = 0.46, mast activated p = 0.90.

**Cohort differences:**
- Gide includes ipilimumab + anti-PD1 patients; Riaz is anti-PD1 only.
- Processing and scale differ between cohorts, and I did no harmonization.
- The subgroups were learned on Gide only.
- Response definitions were taken as given from the clinical table.

**Deconvolution:**
- Only 4 methods were used (no CIBERSORTx).
- The 1e6 rescaling over a filtered gene set affects methods that work on an absolute scale.
- The low Gide totals remain unexplained.

**Not checked:**
- I did not check whether any Gide patients appear in both treatment arms, which would leak information across CV folds.

## Step 3 - Export existing results to a standard format (no recomputation)
## Run from the results/ directory

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(jsonlite))

out_dir <- "standard"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

res <- readRDS("model/pipeML_training_Gide.rds")
model_features <- setdiff(colnames(res$Model$trainingData), ".outcome")

## Subgroups of the final model: one row per member feature
comp <- read.csv("model/subgroup_composition_Gide.csv")
comp <- comp[comp$subgroup %in% model_features, ]
subgroups <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(comp)), function(i)
  data.frame(subgroup = comp$subgroup[i], feature = strsplit(comp$members[i], "; ")[[1]])))
write.csv(subgroups, file.path(out_dir, "subgroups_composition.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

cv <- read.csv("model/cv_AUROC_Gide.csv")
write.csv(data.frame(algorithm = cv$model, cv_auroc = cv$Median_AUROC),
          file.path(out_dir, "cv_performance.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

pred <- read.csv("model/test_predictions_Riaz.csv")
write.csv(data.frame(patient = pred$sample, probability_R = pred$prob_responder),
          file.path(out_dir, "test_predictions.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

## Cell type: subgroups are named <cell type>_Subgroup.N, raw features <method>_<signature>_<cell type>
imp <- read.csv("model/feature_importance_SHAP.csv")
parts <- strsplit(imp$feature, "_")
cell_type <- ifelse(grepl("_Subgroup\\.", imp$feature),
                    sapply(parts, `[`, 1), sapply(parts, function(p) p[length(p)]))
write.csv(data.frame(feature = imp$feature, cell_type = cell_type, importance = imp$mean_abs_shap),
          file.path(out_dir, "feature_importance.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

shap <- readRDS("model/shap_values_Gide.rds")
write.csv(data.frame(patient = rownames(shap), shap, check.names = FALSE),
          file.path(out_dir, "shap_values.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

info <- list(selected_algorithm = res$Model$method, training_cohort = "Gide", test_cohort = "Riaz",
             features_built_inside_cv_folds = TRUE, cv_folds = 5, cv_repeats = 10,
             metric = "AUROC", cibersortx = FALSE)
write_json(info, file.path(out_dir, "info.json"), auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)

All six files were exported to `results/standard/`. Nothing was recomputed and no existing file was changed; I only reformatted saved results with a new script, `scripts/03_export_standard.R`. No item was skipped.

- **`subgroups_composition.csv`**: 147 rows covering the 65 subgroups that are features of the final model. These come from the Gide-only subgrouping saved as the training output; 4 subgroups that pipeML dropped before modelling are not included.
- **`cv_performance.csv`**: 11 algorithms, with the median cross-validation AUROC in Gide.
- **`test_predictions.csv`**: 51 Riaz patients from the main random-forest model. Sample IDs are exactly as in the input file.
- **`feature_importance.csv`**: 151 features, with importance as the mean absolute SHAP value. `cell_type` is not a saved result: I took it from each feature name (the part before `_Subgroup.N`, or the last part of a raw feature name).
- **`shap_values.csv`**: 73 Gide training patients × 151 features. The patient names are the original Gide IDs, without the `X` prefix multideconv added.
- **`info.json`**: random forest (`rf`), trained on Gide and tested on Riaz, features built inside the CV folds, 5 folds × 10 repeats, AUROC, no CIBERSORTx.
